hints: Remember $R_f$ = distance moved by spot divided by distance moved by solvent front, then match your estimated values to the table.
walkthrough:
Measure distances from the baseline**
Picture the plate with the baseline at 0 cm and the solvent front at about 5.0 cm. Spot A has travelled about 3.5 cm up, spot B only about 1.4 to 1.5 cm up. You can estimate this straight from the scale on the left.

Match to the table**
Work out $R_f = \frac{\text{distance by amino acid}}{\text{distance by solvent}}$. For A, $R_f \approx 3.5/5.0 = 0.70$, which matches leucine at 0.71. For B, $R_f \approx 1.45/5.0 = 0.29$, which matches glutamic acid at 0.29.
Final answer: Spot A is leucine ($R_f$ approx 0.71) and spot B is glutamic acid ($R_f$ approx 0.29).

hints: Think about what a larger $R_f$ means in terms of how much time the spot spends dissolved in the moving solvent compared to stuck on the stationary phase.
walkthrough:
Link $R_f$ to solubility**
Amino acids are polar molecules with $\text{NH}_2$ and $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ groups that can hydrogen bond. If you make the moving solvent more polar, these polar solutes dissolve better in it and are carried further up the plate instead of staying adsorbed on the polar stationary phase.

Predict the change**
Greater affinity for the mobile phase means greater distance travelled in the same time, so $R_f$ increases for all the amino acids.
Final answer: $R_f$ values increase because the amino acids are more soluble in the more polar mobile phase and form stronger interactions with it.

hints: Focus on which group in $\text{H}_2\text{NCH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ acts as a base toward $\text{HCl}$ and which acts as an acid toward $\text{NaOH}$.
Remember the amine forms an alkylammonium salt with acid, while the carboxylic acid forms a carboxylate salt plus water with base.
walkthrough:
Acting as a base with HCl**
The lone pair on $\text{NH}_2$ accepts a proton from the strong acid $\text{HCl}$. The $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ group is untouched. You get the cation $\text{H}_3\text{N}^+\text{CH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ with $\text{Cl}^-$ as counter ion: $$\text{H}_2\text{NCH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{H} + \text{HCl} \rightarrow \text{Cl}^-\text{H}_3\text{N}^+\text{CH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{H}$$

Acting as an acid with NaOH**
Now the $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ group donates its proton to $\text{OH}^-$. The $\text{NH}_2$ group is untouched. You get the carboxylate salt plus water: $$\text{H}_2\text{NCH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{H} + \text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{NCH}_2\text{CO}_2^-\text{Na}^+ + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$ This pair of reactions shows glycine is amphoteric.

Final answer: $\text{H}_2\text{NCH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{H} + \text{HCl} \rightarrow \text{Cl}^-\text{H}_3\text{N}^+\text{CH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{H}$
$\text{H}_2\text{NCH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{H} + \text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{NCH}_2\text{CO}_2^-\text{Na}^+ + \text{H}_2\text{O}$

hints: Draw glycine with both charges present, a positive charge on nitrogen and a negative charge on oxygen, giving zero overall charge.
Think of it as an internal acid-base reaction where the $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ proton moves to the $\text{NH}_2$ lone pair within the same molecule.
walkthrough:
Draw the dipolar ion**
In water, glycine does not stay as neutral $\text{H}_2\text{NCH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{H}$. It exists as $$\text{H}_3\text{N}^+\text{CH}_2\text{CO}_2^-$$ with a full positive charge on N and a full negative charge on O, so the overall charge is zero. This is the zwitterion.

Explain the internal transfer**
The carboxylic acid end is acidic enough to lose its proton, and the amine end is basic enough to gain a proton. So the $\text{H}^+$ moves directly from $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ to $\text{NH}_2$ in the same molecule, giving $\text{NH}_3^+$ and $\text{CO}_2^-$.

Final answer: Zwitterion: $\text{H}_3\text{N}^+\text{CH}_2\text{CO}_2^-$
Formed by transfer of a proton from the $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ group to the $\text{NH}_2$ group within the molecule.

hints: Keep three groups fixed on the given 3D template and swap only the wedge and dashed bonds for $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ to create the non-superimposable mirror image.
walkthrough:
Build non-superimposable mirror images**
Alanine has a chiral carbon bonded to $\text{CH}_3$, $\text{NH}_2$, $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ and $\text{H}$. Draw the two forms as exact mirror images. If the left structure has $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ on the solid wedge coming out toward you, the right structure must have $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ on the hashed wedge going away from you, with the other groups mirrored. These are enantiomers.

Final answer: Two mirror image structures of $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(NH}_2\text{)CO}_2\text{H}$ with opposite 3D arrangement at the chiral C, one with $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ on wedge and one with $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ on dashed bond.

hints: Identify the reaction type when $\text{Cl}$ attached to carbon is replaced by $\text{NH}_2$ using excess ammonia.
Recall the specific conditions needed to keep volatile ammonia in contact with the halogenoacid for substitution.
walkthrough:
Choose ammonia as nucleophile**
You need to replace $\text{Cl}$ in $\text{CH}_3\text{CHClCO}_2\text{H}$ by $\text{NH}_2$ to make alanine. Use excess $\text{NH}_3$ dissolved in ethanol, heated in a sealed tube under pressure so the ammonia does not escape. The lone pair on $\text{NH}_3$ attacks the $\text{C-Cl}$ carbon.

Name the pathway**
The $\text{C-Cl}$ bond breaks heterolytically and $\text{Cl}^-$ leaves as $\text{NH}_3$ bonds to carbon, followed by deprotonation to give the amine. This is nucleophilic substitution.

Final answer: Reagents and conditions: $\text{NH}_3$ in ethanol, heat in a sealed tube.
Mechanism: nucleophilic substitution.

hints: Order the three acids by counting electron withdrawing $\text{Cl}$ atoms, most $\text{Cl}$ means strongest acid.
Think about how electronegative $\text{Cl}$ pulls electron density away from the $\text{O-H}$ bond through the sigma framework.
Link this pull to how easily $\text{H}^+$ is lost and how stable the resulting $\text{COO}^-$ anion becomes.
walkthrough:
State the acidity order**
More $\text{Cl}$ atoms means stronger acid. So: $$\text{Cl}_3\text{CCO}_2\text{H} > \text{ClCH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{H} > \text{CH}_3\text{CO}_2\text{H}$$ Trichloroethanoic acid is strongest, ethanoic acid is weakest.

Explain the inductive pull of chlorine**
$\text{Cl}$ is highly electronegative. It withdraws electron density through sigma bonds, the negative inductive (-I) effect. Three $\text{Cl}$ atoms pull much more strongly than one $\text{Cl}$, while $\text{CH}_3$ actually pushes electrons toward the $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ group.

Connect to bond weakening and anion stability**
Pulling electrons away from the $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ group weakens the $\text{O-H}$ bond, so $\text{H}^+$ is lost more easily. It also spreads and stabilises the negative charge left on $\text{COO}^-$ after dissociation. That is why chloro acids dissociate further. In $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ with no -I group, the $\text{O-H}$ stays stronger and the anion is less stabilised.

Final answer: Acidity: $\text{Cl}_3\text{CCO}_2\text{H} > \text{ClCH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{H} > \text{CH}_3\text{CO}_2\text{H}$.
$\text{Cl}$ is electronegative and electron withdrawing by the negative inductive effect, and $\text{Cl}_3\text{CCO}_2\text{H}$ has three $\text{Cl}$ atoms.
This weakens the $\text{O-H}$ bond so it ionises more readily and stabilises the negative charge on the $\text{COO}^-$ anion, whereas $\text{CH}_3$ is electron donating and strengthens the $\text{O-H}$ bond.

hints: List the functional groups available: serine has $\text{OH}$, $\text{NH}_2$ and $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$, alanine has $\text{NH}_2$ and $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$, so condensation can give ester or amide links.
For the ester, join the serine $\text{OH}$ to the alanine $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ with loss of water.
For the two amides, join $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ of one amino acid to $\text{NH}_2$ of the other in both possible directions to make two different dipeptides.
walkthrough:
Form the ester isomer**
Serine has a side chain $\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ that alanine lacks. The $\text{OH}$ of serine can react with the $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ of alanine, eliminating $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ to give an ester link $\text{COOCH}_2$. This gives: $$\text{H}_2\text{NCH(CH}_3\text{)COOCH}_2\text{CH(NH}_2\text{)CO}_2\text{H}$$ Both $\text{NH}_2$ groups remain free.

Form dipeptide serine-alanine**
An amide or peptide link forms between $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ and $\text{NH}_2$ with loss of $\text{H}_2\text{O}$. If serine provides the $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ and alanine provides the $\text{NH}_2$, you get: $$\text{HOCH}_2\text{CH(NH}_2\text{)CONHCH(CH}_3\text{)CO}_2\text{H}$$

Form dipeptide alanine-serine**
Swap the roles. If alanine provides the $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ and serine provides the $\text{NH}_2$, you get the reverse sequence: $$\text{H}_2\text{NCH(CH}_3\text{)CONHCH(CH}_2\text{OH)CO}_2\text{H}$$ These two dipeptides are structural isomers because the $\text{CONH}$ unit points in opposite directions.

Final answer: Ester: $\text{H}_2\text{NCH(CH}_3\text{)COOCH}_2\text{CH(NH}_2\text{)CO}_2\text{H}$
Dipeptide 1: $\text{HOCH}_2\text{CH(NH}_2\text{)CONHCH(CH}_3\text{)CO}_2\text{H}$
Dipeptide 2: $\text{H}_2\text{NCH(CH}_3\text{)CONHCH(CH}_2\text{OH)CO}_2\text{H}$
